overview.title: int8 quantization: the idea and abs-max scaling
overview.chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world
overview.section: 18.3 Speeding up training and inference with lower-precision computation
overview.main_topic: Converting a trained float32 model's matmuls to int8: scale inputs into [-127, 127], multiply in int8, cast back and divide by the product of scales.
overview.central_idea: Because matmul is linear, you can scale its inputs, run it in fast int8 arithmetic and exactly undo the scaling on the output; the only error comes from rounding the scaled inputs to integers. The abs-max scheme picks each tensor's scale so its largest value maps to 127.
overview.importance: int8 quantization is a standard way to make inference faster and models about 4x smaller than float32; understanding the math tells you where its accuracy loss comes from.
learning_objectives: State when float8 is worth using, per the end of section 18.3.5.
Explain the goal of int8 quantization of an already-trained model.
Derive why scaling matmul inputs and dividing the output by the product of the scales recovers the original result.
Explain why naive casting to int8 is destructive and how abs-max scaling fixes it.
Read the `abs_max_quantize` function line by line.

summary:
The page first concludes the float8 discussion from p.584: float8 training is viable only for very large models (typically over 5B parameters) on large, recent GPUs such as the NVIDIA H100, and is rarely used outside foundation-model training runs.

Section 18.3.6 then introduces **`int8` quantization**. Beyond running inference in float16 (or float8), you can take an already trained float32 model and convert its weights to a lower-precision dtype, typically `int8`, while preserving the numerical correctness of the forward pass as much as possible.

The math is simple. Scale every `matmul` input tensor by a factor so its coefficients fit the int8 range `[-127, 127]`, cast to int8, perform the `matmul` in int8 (faster than float16), cast the output back to float32 and **divide by the product of the input scaling factors**. Because `matmul` is linear, the unscaling cancels the scaling exactly; the only accuracy loss comes from rounding when the scaled inputs are cast to int8.

The worked example uses `x = [[0.1, 0.9], [1.2, -0.8]]` and `kernel = [[-0.1, -2.2], [1.1, 0.7]]`. Casting these directly to int8 would be destructive: `x` would become `[[0, 0], [1, 0]]`. Instead the book applies **abs-max scaling**: compute the maximum absolute value of the tensor, set `scale = 127 / (abs_max + 1e-7)` (the epsilon prevents division by zero), multiply, then round and clip to `[-127, 127]` (rounding and clipping first is more accurate than casting directly). The function continues on p.586 with the cast to int8 and the return of both the integer tensor and its scale.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Scale all matmul inputs so their coefficients fit [-127, 127], cast to int8, matmul in int8, cast the output to float32 and divide by the product of the input scaling factors. Linearity makes the unscaling cancel the scaling, so the only error is rounding during the cast.

concepts.name: int8 quantization
concepts.definition: Converting float tensors (weights and, at run time, activations) to 8-bit integers plus scale factors so that matmuls can run in integer arithmetic.
concepts.intuition: Measure everything in a coarser unit that fits a small integer counter, and remember the unit.
concepts.technical: $q = \mathrm{clip}(\mathrm{round}(s\,v), -127, 127)$ with $s = 127/\max|v|$; matmul outputs are divided by $s_x s_W$.
concepts.significance: Faster inference than float16 and 4x smaller weights than float32.
concepts.misconception: Quantization does not retrain or change the function's intent; the error comes only from rounding.

concepts.name: Abs-max scaling
concepts.definition: Choosing a tensor's quantization scale as the int range maximum (127) divided by the tensor's maximum absolute value.
concepts.intuition: Stretch the values so the biggest one just touches the edge of the integer range.
concepts.technical: scale = 127 / (max|v| + 1e-7); the epsilon avoids division by zero for an all-zero tensor.
concepts.significance: Simple, symmetric, and uses the full int8 range for the largest value.
concepts.example: kernel abs max is 2.2, so scale ≈ 57.73 and -2.2 maps to -127.
concepts.misconception: Abs-max does not guarantee small error for every value: outliers make the step size large for all others.

concepts.name: Linearity of matmul
concepts.definition: Scaling either input of a matmul by a scalar scales the output by the same scalar.
concepts.intuition: Doubling every price doubles every total bill.
concepts.technical: $(s_x x)(s_W W) = s_x s_W (xW)$ for scalars $s_x, s_W$.
concepts.significance: It is why the unscaling 'cancels out the initial scaling'.
concepts.example: Non-linear ops like softmax do not have this property, which is why quantization targets matmul-heavy layers.
concepts.misconception: Linearity cancels the scale, not the rounding error.

math.title: Abs-max quantization of a tensor
math.source_text: abs_max = ops.max(ops.abs(value), keepdims=True); scale = ops.divide(127, abs_max + 1e-7); scaled_value = ops.clip(ops.round(value * scale), -127, 127)

variables.meaning: the float tensor to quantize (x or kernel)
the integer-valued tensor, later cast to int8

math.operations: Max of absolute values, division, elementwise multiplication, rounding to nearest integer, clipping.
math.purpose: Map the tensor onto the int8 grid using the whole symmetric range.
math.interpretation: The step size in original units is $1/s = \max|v|/127$; rounding error per entry is at most half of that.
math.intuition: The largest-magnitude entry becomes ±127; everything else scales proportionally.
math.numerical_example: For `x`: $\max|x| = 1.2$, $s_x = 127/1.2 \approx 105.83$. $s_x x = [[10.58, 95.25],[127.0, -84.67]]$, rounded: $[[11, 95],[127, -85]]$. For `kernel`: $\max = 2.2$, $s_W \approx 57.73$; $s_W W = [[-5.77, -127.0],[63.50, 40.41]]$, rounded: $[[-6, -127],[64, 40]]$. Subtlety (beyond the book): $1.1 \times 127/2.2$ is exactly the tie 63.5; in float32 the product comes out as 63.5 and rounds (half-to-even) to 64, matching the book's printed output on p.586, whereas float64 with the 1e-7 epsilon gives 63.49999... and rounds to 63. Max rounding error for x is $0.5/105.83 \approx 0.0047$.

code.title: abs_max_quantize (first part; continues on p.586)
code.original_code:
def abs_max_quantize(value):
    abs_max = ops.max(ops.abs(value), keepdims=True)
    scale = ops.divide(127, abs_max + 1e-7)
    scaled_value = value * scale
    scaled_value = ops.clip(ops.round(scaled_value), -127, 127)
code.what_it_does: Computes the abs-max scale of a tensor and maps the tensor onto integers in [-127, 127]. On p.586 the function casts the result to int8 and returns it together with the scale.

line_explanations.explanation: Defines the quantizer for any float tensor.
Callout: 'Max of absolute value of the tensor'. `keepdims=True` keeps a shape like (1, 1) so it broadcasts against `value`.
Callout: 'Scale is max of int range divided by max of tensor (1e-7 is to avoid dividing by 0)'.
Callout: 'Scales the value'. The largest-magnitude entry becomes ±127.

Callout: 'Rounding and clipping first is more accurate than directly casting.' A cast would truncate toward zero; rounding picks the nearest integer, and clipping guards against values just outside the range.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: a float tensor. After line 5: a float tensor holding integer values in [-127, 127] (still float dtype until the cast on p.586).
code.algorithm: abs-max symmetric per-tensor quantization: s = 127/max|v|, q = clip(round(s·v)).

parameters.name: 1e-7
parameters.role: Epsilon to avoid division by zero.
Maximum of the symmetric int8 range.

pitfalls: Without `keepdims=True`, the max would be a scalar; that also broadcasts, but keepdims keeps a consistent rank for later per-axis variants.
A single outlier makes the scale small for every other entry (beyond the book).
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: reproduce the scaled values by hand with NumPy
import numpy as np
x = np.array([[0.1, 0.9], [1.2, -0.8]])
s = 127 / (np.abs(x).max() + 1e-7)
print(s)                                 # ~105.83
print(np.clip(np.round(x * s), -127, 127))  # [[11, 95], [127, -85]]
print(x.astype(np.int8))                 # naive cast: [[0, 0], [1, 0]]

deeper.title: Where the speed and memory gains come from
deeper.body:
- **Memory/bandwidth**: an int8 weight is 1 byte vs. 4 for float32 and 2 for float16; for large models inference is often limited by how fast weights stream from memory, so this alone speeds things up.
- **Arithmetic**: integer matrix units can perform more int8 multiply-adds per cycle than float16 ones on many accelerators.
- **Overhead**: computing abs-max, scaling, rounding, clipping and casting are cheap elementwise ops compared with an $O(n^3)$ matmul (p.586 makes this point).

deeper.title: Truncation vs. rounding
deeper.body: Casting truncates toward zero: $0.9 \to 0$, $-0.8 \to 0$. Rounding chooses the nearest integer. After scaling, x·s = 95.25 truncates and rounds to 95 (same), but 10.58 truncates to 10 and rounds to 11, and -84.67 truncates to -84 and rounds to -85. Truncation has a systematic bias toward zero; rounding error is unbiased and at most 0.5 grid steps, which is why the callout says rounding first is more accurate.

questions.question: Why can the output of an int8 matmul be converted back to the correct float result?
options: Because int8 has the same range as float32
Because matmul is linear, so dividing by the product of the input scales cancels the scaling
Because the rounding errors cancel out on average
Because the kernel is stored in float32
questions.answer: Because matmul is linear, so dividing by the product of the input scales cancels the scaling
questions.explanation: This is the book's argument. int8's range is tiny; rounding errors do not cancel exactly (they are the residual error); the kernel is quantized to int8 too.

questions.question: Using abs-max scaling, compute the scale for kernel = [[-0.1, -2.2], [1.1, 0.7]] and its quantized values.
What does x become if cast directly to int8 without scaling, and why?
questions.answer: [[0, 0], [1, 0]], because casting truncates toward zero and most entries have magnitude below 1.
questions.explanation: Given on the page; truncation maps 0.1, 0.9 and -0.8 to 0 and 1.2 to 1.

questions.question: Why does abs_max_quantize round and clip before casting, instead of casting directly?
questions.answer: Casting truncates, introducing a bias toward zero and up to a full grid step of error; rounding gives at most half a step. Clipping guarantees values stay within [-127, 127].
questions.explanation: The callout says rounding and clipping first is more accurate than direct casting.

questions.question: The text says [-127, 127] is 'a total of 256 possible values'. Is that right?
